work_or_witness: Bari Gongju, regional variants documented by the Academy of Korean Studies
description: Abandoned seventh daughter who seeks the life-giving water needed to save her parents and is associated with guiding the dead in ritual performance.

power_traditions.term: guidance of the dead in ritual narrative
power_traditions.note: Functional comparison only; the witness describes a ritual role, not a game-like power system.

cosmologies_and_realms.note: The source stresses horizontal rather than a universal vertical underworld model.

metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.term: mangja cheondo gut (rite guiding the dead)
metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.note: Partial functional mapping; a living ritual must not be reduced to a transport mechanic.

narrative_archetypes.note: Analytic plot coordinate only; variants differ.

canon_status: attested across documented regional ritual variants

supports: Bari is abandoned, obtains medicinal water after a required cost, saves her parents, and is known as a spirit guiding the dead.

comparison_cautions: Bari Gongju/Baridegi is a regionally variable ritual narrative; this record does not supply a universal version or equate her ritual status with a generic psychopomp class.

work_or_witness: Bari Gongju, Central-Western variants documented by the Academy of Korean Studies
description: Named guardian of the medicinal water and Bari’s destined partner in the Central-Western regional form.

metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.note: The source gives a required act/cost but differs by variant.

supports: Mujangseung appears as medicinal-water guardian and becomes Bari’s lifelong partner in this regional form.

comparison_cautions: This named guardian is regional, not a figure shared by all Bari variants.

description: Husband of Yeosan Buin who travels to Odong, is deceived by Gwiil’s daughter, and later becomes the pillar deity in the Jeju household-deity origin narrative.

states_and_transformations.note: Office/deity outcome is source-specific, not a generic transformation tier.

supports: Nam Seonbi is Yeosan Buin’s husband, is deceived by Gwiil’s daughter, and becomes jumokjisin after death.

comparison_cautions: A household deity origin in a Jeju ritual narrative is not evidence for a universal Korean household pantheon.

description: Nam Seonbi’s first wife, murdered by Gwiil’s daughter, revived with flowers from Seocheon Flower Garden, and installed as the kitchen deity in this narrative.

being_types.note: Partial household-spirit comparison only; the identity is a narrative-specific installation.

states_and_transformations.note: Direct narrative event; it does not establish a general resurrection rule.

supports: Yeosan Buin is drowned, her sons obtain resurrection flowers, and she is revived and installed as jowangsin.

comparison_cautions: Jowangsin has varying Korean and transregional religious histories; this record is restricted to the Jeju narrative.

description: Uniquely designated daughter of Gwiil who seduces Nam Seonbi, kills Yeosan Buin, and ultimately becomes the outhouse deity in the narrative.

states_and_transformations.note: Source-specific office outcome, not a generic creature change.

canon_status: uniquely designated agent in Jeju ritual narrative

supports: Gwiil’s daughter seduces Nam Seonbi, murders Yeosan Buin, and becomes Cheukdo Buin after her death.

comparison_cautions: The source preserves a designation rather than an independent personal name; retained because it uniquely identifies an acting individual in this one narrative.

description: The clever youngest son who recognizes the impostor, obtains resurrection flowers with his brothers, and becomes the front gate deity Ilmunjeon.

supports: The youngest son detects the deception, helps secure resurrection flowers, and becomes the front gate deity.

comparison_cautions: The other six brothers are not entered because this account supplies no individual names for them.

description: Human official recruited by Yeomra Wang whose soul is taken to the underworld; he is then appointed to seize and summon the dead.

being_types.note: Partial functional comparison, not a claim that chasa equals a generic psychopomp species.

states_and_transformations.note: The source describes division of soul and body; this mapping is analytic only.

cosmologies_and_realms.note: Direct underworld journey; no claim of a uniform Korean afterlife.

citations.locator: Contents, Yeomra Wang encounter through final appointment
supports: Yeomra Wang takes Gangnim’s soul and appoints him as a chasa who brings people to the underworld.

comparison_cautions: Gangnim’s underworld office belongs to this Jeju narrative and ritual context; do not treat it as a standardized fantasy job.

description: Underworld king who negotiates for Gangnim’s service, takes his soul, and appoints him a chasa.

being_types.note: Functional deity mapping only; Buddhist and shamanic layers must not be collapsed.

cosmologies_and_realms.note: The narrative gives an underworld ruler, not a full court cosmology.

citations.locator: Contents, Gangnim’s audience with Yeomra Wang
supports: Yeomra Wang arranges for Gangnim’s soul and makes him a chasa.

comparison_cautions: The Yeomra name participates in wider East Asian Buddhist underworld vocabularies, but this record only reports its function in Chasabonpuri.

description: Official who refuses Yeomra Wang’s request to loan Gangnim, then chooses Gangnim’s body when offered a division of body and soul.

citations.locator: Contents, Yeomra Wang’s request and body/soul proposal
supports: Gimchi Wonim refuses to lend Gangnim and selects Gangnim’s body in Yeomra Wang’s proposed division.

comparison_cautions: Official title and spelling follow the cited Korean scholarly reference; no historical-person identification is asserted.

description: A three-thousand-year-old figure whom Gangnim identifies through a riddle-like exchange and takes to the underworld.

supports: Gangnim uses the charcoal-washing exchange to identify Dongbangsak and brings him to the underworld.

comparison_cautions: The account names Dongbangsak but this pass does not infer a stable transregional biography from the episode.

description: Son of the dead King Jinji and Tohwa-nyeo who commands ghosts, has Gil Dal killed, and is subsequently invoked in an apotropaic formula.

power_traditions.note: Functional comparison only; not an imported spell-school classification.

metaphysical_laws_and_rituals.note: The account describes an apotropaic formula, not a general exorcism ruleset.

supports: Bihyeong is born from a dead king’s spirit, commands ghosts, has Gil Dal killed, and becomes an object of ghost-averting belief.

comparison_cautions: This early written account and its later apotropaic reception are not a general taxonomy of Korean spirits.

description: Loyal assistant who turns into a fox and flees; Bihyeong has ghosts capture and kill him.

power_traditions.note: Directly stated for this named agent; no general gumiho equivalence is implied.

supports: Gil Dal transforms into a fox and flees; Bihyeong orders ghosts to capture and kill him.

comparison_cautions: Gil Dal’s fox transformation is evidence for this account only. It does not identify him as a gumiho or define all Korean fox narratives.

description: Named supernatural builder in the Bihyeongrang account, credited with building a bridge overnight and constructing a great hall.

supports: Duduri’s supernatural power includes building a bridge overnight and a great hall.

comparison_cautions: The source’s later belief/history discussion is not proof of one uniform being type.

description: Deposed Silla king who returns after death in the appearance of his living self and fathers Bihyeong with Tohwa-nyeo.

states_and_transformations.note: Narrative description only; not a generic revenant taxonomy.

supports: After his deposition and death, King Jinji returns to Tohwa-nyeo in his former appearance and Bihyeong is born.

comparison_cautions: This text’s supernatural narrative is not a historical claim about the king’s life.

description: Woman who refuses King Jinji while her husband is alive, receives the dead king after her husband’s death, and gives birth to Bihyeong.

supports: Tohwa-nyeo refuses the king while married, is visited after her husband’s death, and bears Bihyeong.

comparison_cautions: The source recounts a literary-religious narrative; do not interpret it as a documentary biography.
